
### Pen-and-Pencil {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-dutch-book}
## Dutch Book and Coherence

A racetrack analyst states her personal probabilities for an upcoming three-horse race between Alpha, Beta, and Gamma, where exactly one horse wins (no ties, no scratches). She quotes two-sided prices in the betting sense of this chapter: for any of the three outcomes, she will, at her stated price, both buy and sell a contract paying \$1 if that horse wins and \$0 otherwise, in any quantity you request. Her quotes are
$$
P(\text{Alpha wins}) = 0.50, \qquad P(\text{Beta wins}) = 0.35, \qquad P(\text{Gamma wins}) = 0.25.
$$

a) The events \{Alpha wins, Beta wins, Gamma wins\} are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Which axiom of probability do these quoted prices violate, and why must that axiom hold for any coherent assignment of probabilities to a partition of the sample space?
a) You decide to exploit the mispricing. Should you buy or sell contracts on all three horses, and why? Using a common stake $S = \pm 100$ (state the sign), find your net cash flow in each of the three possible worlds (Alpha wins, Beta wins, Gamma wins) and confirm that your profit is identical and strictly positive, no matter which horse wins. This is the explicit Dutch book.
a) Generalize part (b). A bettor takes an equal, signed stake $S$ on each of $k$ mutually exclusive, exhaustive events with quoted prices $P(A_1), \ldots, P(A_k)$: paying $P(A_i) S$ now for contract $i$, and receiving $S$ back on whichever event occurs. Show that the guaranteed gain is
$$
G = S\left(1 - \sum_{i=1}^k P(A_i)\right),
$$
the same value in every possible world. Use this formula to explain (i) why $\sum_i P(A_i) > 1$ is exploitable by selling ($S<0$), (ii) why $\sum_i P(A_i) < 1$ is exploitable by buying ($S>0$), and (iii) why no Dutch book of this kind exists when $\sum_i P(A_i) = 1$.
a) The analyst revises her quote to $P(\text{Gamma wins}) = 0.15$, leaving the other two prices unchanged. Is the book now coherent? Use your formula from part (c) to explain why the equal-stake construction can no longer turn a riskless profit.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) The three outcomes partition the sample space: mutually exclusive, since only one horse wins, and exhaustive, since some horse must win. Coherence requires the probabilities of a partition to sum to exactly $1$, a consequence of normalization ($P(\Omega)=1$) together with finite additivity ($P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ for disjoint events, extended across the whole partition). Here
$$
P(\text{Alpha}) + P(\text{Beta}) + P(\text{Gamma}) = 0.50 + 0.35 + 0.25 = 1.10 \neq 1,
$$
so the quoted prices violate finite additivity.

a) The three prices sum to $1.10 > 1$, so the contracts are collectively overpriced: buying all three would cost \$1.10 for a guaranteed payout of only \$1, a sure loss for the buyer. The exploitable side is therefore to sell (write) equal exposure on all three horses. Take $S=-100$: you sell \$100 of exposure on each horse, receiving $P(A_i)\times 100$ from the analyst up front for each contract, and owing \$100 on whichever contract turns out to be the winner (the other two expire worthless). You collect
$$
100(0.50+0.35+0.25) = \$110
$$
up front, and pay out exactly \$100 on the single winning contract, whichever horse wins:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Alpha wins:} &\quad 110 - 100 = +10 \\
\text{Beta wins:} &\quad 110 - 100 = +10 \\
\text{Gamma wins:} &\quad 110 - 100 = +10
\end{aligned}
$$
The profit is exactly \$10 regardless of which horse wins: a Dutch book against the analyst, who loses \$10 for sure.

a) Paying $P(A_i)S$ now for each of the $k$ contracts and receiving $S$ back on the one event that occurs,
$$
G = \underbrace{S}_{\text{payout on the winning contract}} - \underbrace{S\sum_{i=1}^k P(A_i)}_{\text{total paid up front}} = S\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^k P(A_i)\right).
$$
Exactly one of the $k$ events occurs, so this is the net gain in every possible world: it does not depend on which $A_i$ occurs, and is therefore riskless.

(i) If $\sum_i P(A_i) > 1$, the factor $\left(1-\sum_i P(A_i)\right)$ is negative, so $G>0$ requires $S<0$: sell equal stakes on every outcome, as in part (b).

(ii) If $\sum_i P(A_i) < 1$, the factor is positive, so $G>0$ requires $S>0$: buy equal stakes on every outcome. This is the mirror-image case, illustrated earlier in the chapter with two events summing to $0.9$.

(iii) If $\sum_i P(A_i) = 1$, then $G = S \times 0 = 0$ for every choice of $S$, so the equal-stake construction cannot produce a riskless profit in either direction. This is finite additivity: $\sum_i P(A_i)=1$ is necessary for coherence, since by (i) and (ii) any other value is exploitable, and, combined with the determinant argument of the [Appendix](#sec-dutch-book) covering arbitrary, unequal stakes, sufficient as well.

a) With prices $0.50, 0.35, 0.15$, the sum is $\sum_i P(A_i) = 1.00$. By part (c), $G = S(1-1) = 0$ for every stake $S$, so selling or buying equal exposure across the three horses now breaks even in every possible world: this construction yields no arbitrage. A full proof that no combination of stakes, equal or not, can produce a Dutch book once $\sum_i P(A_i)=1$ and each $P(A_i)\in[0,1]$ follows the same determinant argument used in the [Appendix](#sec-dutch-book) for two events and their complement.
:::
:::

## Joint Distributions
 
A credit card company collects data on $10{,}000$ users. The data contained two variables: an indicator of the customer status: whether they are in default (`def` = 1) or if they are current with their payments (`def` = 0). Moreover, they have a measure of their loan balance relative to income with three categories: a low balance (`bal`=1), medium (`bal`=2), and high (`bal`=3). The data are given in the following table:

  ----- ------- -----
          def   
   bal     0      1
    1    8,940   64
    2     651    136
    3     76     133
  ----- ------- -----

a) Compute the marginal distribution of customer status
b) What is the conditional distribution of bal given `def` = 1
c) Make a prediction for the status of a customer with a high balance

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**: 

a) The marginal distribution of customer status is given by the sum of the rows of the table. 
```{r}
d = data.frame(def0=c(8940,651,76),def1=c(64,136,133),row.names = c("bal1","bal2","bal3"))
apply(d,2,sum)/10000
```
b) The conditional distribution of `bal` given `def` = 1 is given by the ratio of the joint (elements of the table) to the marginal (sum of the `def` = 1 column)
```{r}
d[,"def1"]/sum(d[,"def1"])
```
c) The prediction for the status of a customer with a high balance is the conditional distribution over `def` = 1, given balance.
$$
P(def\mid bal) = \frac{P(def \text{ and } bal)}{P(bal)}
$$
```{r}
balmarginal = apply(d,1,sum)
d1b3 = d["bal3","def1"]/balmarginal["bal3"]
d1b1 = d["bal1","def1"]/balmarginal["bal1"]
print(d1b3)
print(d1b1)
# The ratio is 
d1b3/d1b1
```
Person with high balance has 63% chance of being in default, while a person with low balance has 0.7% chance of being in default, 90-times less likely!
:::
:::

## Marginal
The table below is taken from the Hoff text and shows the joint distribution of occupations taken from a 1983 study of social mobility by @logan1983multivariate. Each cell is P(father's occupation, son's occupation).
```{r}
d = data.frame(farm = c(0.018,0.002,0.001,0.001,0.001),operatives=c(0.035,0.112,0.066,0.018,0.029),craftsman=c(0.031,0.064,0.094,0.019,0.032),sales=c(0.008,0.032,0.032,0.010,0.043),professional=c(0.018,0.069,0.084,0.051,0.130), row.names = c("farm","operative","craftsman","sales","professional"))
d %>% knitr::kable()
```


a) Find the marginal distribution of fathers' occupations.
a) Find the marginal distribution of sons' occupations.
a) Find the conditional distribution of the son's occupation given that the father is a farmer.
a) Find the conditional distribution of the father's occupation given that the son is a farmer.
a) Comment on these results. What do they say about changes in farming in the population from which these data are drawn?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) 
```{r}
apply(d,1,sum)
```
b) 
```{r}
apply(d,2,sum)
```
c) 
```{r}
d["farm",]/sum(d["farm",])
```
d) 
```{r}
d[,"farm"]/sum(d[,"farm"])
```
e) 
```{r}
dd = data.frame(son=as.double(d["farm",]/sum(d["farm",])),father=as.double(d[,"farm"]/sum(d[,"farm"])))
barplot(height = t(as.matrix(dd)),beside=TRUE,legend=TRUE, col = c("lightblue", "coral"))
```
The bar chart allows us to visualize the marginal distributions of occupations of fathers and sons. The striking feature of this chart is that in the sons, the proportion of farmers has greatly decreased and the proportion of professionals has increased. From Part d, we see that of the sons who are farmers, 78% had fathers who are farmers. On the other hand, Part c shows that only 16% of the fathers who farmed produced sons who farmed. This is higher than the 2.3% of sons in the general population who became farmers, showing that sons of farmers went into farming at a rate higher than the general population of the study. However, most of the sons of farmers went into another profession. There was a great deal of movement out of farming and very little movement into farming from the fathers' to the sons' generation.


To determine the validity of inference outside the sample, we would need to know more about how the study was designed. We do not know how the sample was selected or what steps were taken to ensure it was representative of the population being studied. We also are not given the sample size, so we don't know the accuracy of our probability estimates. The paper from which the table was taken, cited in the problem, provides more detail on the study.
:::
:::

## Conditional

Netflix surveyed the general population as to the number of hours per week that you used their service. The following table provides the proportions of each category according to whether you are a teenager or adults.

     Hours      Teenager   Adult
  ------------ ---------- -------
      $<4$        0.18     0.20
   $4$ to $6$     0.12     0.32
      $>6$        0.04     0.14

Calculate the following probabilities:

a) Given that you spend $4$ to $6$ hours a week watching movies, what's the probability that you are a teenager?
a) What is the marginal distribution of hours spent watching movies.
a) Are hours spent watching Netflix movies independent of age?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) $\frac{0.12}{0.12+0.32}=0.2727$
a) See Table:

         Hours        Probability
      ------------ -----------------
          $<4$      0.18+0.20=0.38
       $4$ to $6$   0.12+0.32=0.44
          $>6$      0.04+0.14=0.18

a) No, the marginal distribution of hours given you are a teenager or adult are not the same:

| Hours      |   Teenager                           | Adult                                | 
|----------- | ------------------------------------ | -----------------------------------  | 
| $<4$       | $\frac{0.18}{0.18+0.12+0.04}=0.5294$ | $\frac{0.20}{0.20+0.32+0.14}=0.3030$ |

| $>6$       | $\frac{0.04}{0.18+0.12+0.04}=0.1176$ | $\frac{0.14}{0.20+0.32+0.14}=0.2121$ |

## Joint and Conditional

The following probability table relates $Y$, the number of TV shows
watched by the typical student in an evening, to the number of drinks $X$
consumed.

        Y                  
  --- ------ ------ ------ ------
   X    0      1      2      3
   0   0.07   0.09   0.06   0.01
   1   0.07   0.06   0.07   0.01
   2   0.06   0.07   0.14   0.03
   3   0.02   0.04   0.16   0.04
  
a) What is the probability that a student has more than two drinks in
    an evening?
a) What is the probability that a student drink more than the number of
    TV shows they watch?
a) What's the conditional distribution of the number of TV shows
    watched given they consume $3$ drinks?
a) What's the expected number of drinks given they do not watch TV
a) Are drinking and watching TV independent?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) $P(X > 2 ) = 0.26$.
a) $P(X>Y) = 0.42$
a) $P( Y \mid X=3 )$ are given by $( 1/13 , 2/13 , 8/13 , 2/13 )$.
a) $P( X \mid Y=0 )$ are given by $( 7/22 , 7/22 , 3/11 , 1/11 )$ and so $E(X\mid Y=0) = 25/22 = 1.13$
a) No. $P( X = 2 \text{ and } Y=2 )= 0.14 \neq 0.43 \times 0.30 = P(X=2 ) P(Y=2)$
:::

## Conditional Probability

Shipments from an online retailer take between 1 and 7 days to arrive, depending on where they ship from, when they were ordered, the size of the item, etc. Suppose the distribution of delivery times has the following distribution function:

            x              1      2      3      4      5      6     7
  ---------------------- ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ---
    $\mbox{P}(X = x)$                                              
   $\mbox{P}(X \leq x)$   0.10   0.20   0.70   0.75   0.80   0.90   1

a) Fill in the above probability table.
a) What is the conditional probability of a delivery arriving on day
    four given that it did not arrive in the first three days? (Hint:
    find $P(X = 4 \mid X >= 4)$)


::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

$$P(X = 1) = P(X \leq 1) = 0.1$$
$$P(X = 2) = P(X \leq 2) - P(X \leq 1) = 0.2 - 0.1 = 0.1$$
$$P(X = 3) = P(X \leq 3) - P(X \leq 2) = 0.7 - 0.2 = 0.5$$

            x              1      2      3      4      5      6      7
  ---------------------- ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------ ------
    $\mbox{P}(X = x)$     0.10   0.10   0.50   0.05   0.05   0.10   0.10
   $\mbox{P}(X \leq x)$   0.10   0.20   0.70   0.75   0.80   0.90    1

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X >= 4) &= 0.05 + 0.05 + 0.10 + 0.10 = 0.30\\
P(X = 4 \text{ and } X >=4) &= P(X = 4) = 0.05\\
P(X = 4 \mid X >= 4) &= \frac{P(X = 4 \text{ and } X >=4)}{P(X >= 4)} = \frac{0.05}{0.30} = \frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::

## Joint and Conditional

A cable television company has $10000$ subscribers in a suburban community. The company offers two premium channels, HBO and Showtime. Suppose $2750$ subscribers receive HBO and $2050$ receive Showtime and $6200$ do not receive any premium channel.

a) What is the probability that a randomly selected subscriber receives both HBO and Showtime.
a) What is the probability that a randomly selected subscriber receives HBO but not Showtime.

You now obtain a new dataset, categorized by gender, on the proportions of people who watch HBO and Showtime given below

| Cable    | Female | Male |
| :------- | :----- | :--- |
| HBO      | 0.14   | 0.48 |
| Showtime | 0.17   | 0.21 |


c) Conditional on being female, what's the probability you receive HBO?
d) Conditional on being female, what's the probability you receive Showtime?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) We can calculate the  number of people who receive both HBO and Showtime by calculating how many were "double counted" in the HBO and Showtime counts.
```{r}
2750 + 2050 + 6200 - 10000
```
Thus, the answer is $1000/10000 = 0.1$.

a) $\frac{2750-1000}{10000}=\frac{1750}{10000}=0.175$
a) $P(HBO\mid F)=\frac{0.14}{0.14+0.17}=0.4516$
a) $P(Show\mid F)=\frac{0.17}{0.14+0.17}=0.5484$

:::

## Conditionals and Expectations

The following probability table describes the daily sales volume, $X$,
in thousands of dollars for a salesperson for the number of years $Y$ of
sales experience for a particular company.

         Y                  
  ---- ------ ------ ------ ------
   X     1      2      3      4
   10   0.14   0.03   0.03    0
   20   0.05   0.10   0.12   0.07
   30   0.10   0.06   0.25   0.05

a) Verify that this is a legal probability table.
a) What is the probability of at least two years of experience?
a) Calculate the mean daily sales volume
a) Given a salesperson has three years of experience, calculate the mean
    daily sales volume.
a) A salesperson is paid \$1000 per week plus 2% of total sales. What
    is the expected compensation for a salesperson?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) All probabilities are between zero and one, and the entire table
    adds to one
a) $P(Y\geq 2)=0.19+0.40+0.12=0.71$
a) $E(X) = 10 \times 0.20 + 20 \times 0.34 + 30 \times 0.46 = 22.6$,
    that is \$22,600
a) First, the conditional probability distribution $p( X\mid Y)$ is given by, $0.03 /0.4 , 0.12/0.4 , 0.25/0.4$. Hence $E(X\mid Y=3)=10\times 0.075+20\times 0.3+30\times 0.625=25.5,$ that is \$25,500
a) Assuming a 5-day workweek, $E(Comp)=1000+0.02E(X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+X_{5})=1000+0.02\cdot 5\cdot E(X)=1000+0.02\cdot 5\cdot 22600=\$3{,}260$. With a 7-day week, $E(Comp)=1000+0.02\cdot 7\cdot 22600=\$4{,}164$
:::

## Conditional Probability

A super market carried out a survey and found the following
probabilities for people who buy generic products depending on whether
they visit the store frequently or not

                Purchase Generic             
  ------------ ------------------ ---------- -------
     Visit           Often         Sometime   Never
    Frequent          0.10           0.50     0.17
   Infrequent         0.03           0.05     0.15

a) What is the probability that a customer who never buys generics
    visits the store?
a) What is the probability that a customer often purchases generic?
a) Are buying generics and visiting the store independent decisions?
a) What is the conditional distribution of purchasing generics given
    that you frequently visit the store?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) $P ( F \text{ and } N ) + P ( \bar{F} \text{ and } N ) = 0.17 + 0.15 = 0.32$
a) $P( F \text{ and } O ) + P( \bar{F} \text{ and } O ) = 0.10 + 0.03 = 0.13$
a) $P( F \mid S ) = 0.9091 , P( \bar{F} \mid S ) = 0.0909$ and
    $P( F \mid O ) = 0.7692 , P( \bar{F} \mid O ) = 0.2308$. The probabilities
    are not the same so the events are not independent.
a) $P( O \mid F ) = 0.1299 , P( S\mid F) = 0.6494 , P( N \mid F ) = 0.2208$.
:::
:::

## Conditional Probability

Cooper Realty is a small real estate company located in Albany, New
York, specializing primarily in residential listings. They have recently
become interested in determining the likelihood of one of their listings
being sold within a certain number of days. An analysis of recent
company sales of 800 homes produced the following table:

   Days Listed until Sold   Under 20   31-90   Over 90   Total
  ------------------------ ---------- ------- --------- -------
        Under \$50K            50       40       10       100
        \$50-\$100K            20       150      80       250
        \$100-\$150K           20       280      100      400
        Over \$ 150K           10       30       10       50

a) Estimate the probability that a home listed for over 90 days before being sold
a) Estimate the probability that the initial asking price is under \$50K.
a) What is the probability of both of the above happening? Are these two events independent?
a) Assuming that a contract has just been signed to list a home that has an initial asking price of less than \$100K, what is the probability that the home will take Cooper Realty more than 90 days to sell?


::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:
Let $A$ be the event that it takes more than 90 days to sell. Let $B$  denote the event that the initial asking price is under \$50K.

a) $P(A) = ( 10 + 80 + 100 + 10)/800 = 200/800 = 0.25$
a) $P(B) = 100/800 = 0.125$
a) $P( A \text{ and } B ) = 10/800 = 0.0125$
a) First, $P( < \$100K ) = 350/800 = 0.4375$. Secondly, 
$$
P( A \mid < \$100K ) = P( < \$100K \mid A ) P(A)/ P( < \$100K) = (90/200)\times(200/800)/0.4375 = 0.2571
$$
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Probability and Combinations

In 2006, the St. Louis Cardinals and the Detroit Tigers played for the World Series. The two teams play seven games, and the first team to win four games wins the world series.

The Cardinals were leading the series 3--1. Given that each game is independent of another and that the probability of the Cardinals winning any single game is 0.55, what's the probability that they would go on to win the World Series?

In 2012, the St. Louis Cardinals found themselves in a similar situation against the San Francisco Giants in the National League Championships. Now suppose that the probability of the Cardinals winning any single game is 0.45.

How does the probability that they get to the World Series differ from before?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

Leading $3$-$1$, the Cardinals have already won $3$ games and need just $1$ more win, out of at most $3$ remaining games, to clinch the series, while the opponent needs to win all $3$ remaining games to force a $4$-$3$ series win of their own. Since games are independent with $P(\text{Cardinals win a game}) = p$, the Cardinals fail to win the series only if they lose all $3$ remaining games, so
$$
P(\text{Cardinals win series}) = 1 - (1-p)^3.
$$
Equivalently, summing over the game in which they clinch it (win game $5$, or lose game $5$ then win game $6$, or lose games $5$ and $6$ then win game $7$):
$$
P(\text{Cardinals win series}) = p + (1-p)p + (1-p)^2 p = 1 - (1-p)^3.
$$

For $p = 0.55$ (2006, vs. Detroit):
```{r}
1 - (1-0.55)^3
```
$P(\text{win}) = 1-(0.45)^3 = 0.9089$.

For $p = 0.45$ (2012, vs. San Francisco):
```{r}
1 - (1-0.45)^3
```
$P(\text{win}) = 1-(0.55)^3 = 0.8336$.

Because the Cardinals are now the underdog in each individual game ($p=0.45<0.5$), their chance of closing out the series drops from about $90.9$% to about $83.4$%, a decrease of about $7.5$ percentage points (a relative decrease of about $8$%). Historically, this is exactly what happened: the Cardinals closed out Detroit in Game 5 in 2006, while San Francisco came back to win Games 5, 6 and 7 of the 2012 NLCS.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Probability and Lotteries

The Powerball lottery is open to participants across several states. When entering the powerball lottery, a participant selects five numbers from 1-59 and then selects a powerball number from the digits 1-35. In addition, there's a \$1 million payoff for anybody selecting the first five numbers correctly.

a) Show that the odds of winning the Powerball Jackpot are 1 in 175,223,510.
a) Show that the odds of winning the \$1 million are 1 in 5,153,632.

On February 18, 2006, the Jackpot reached \$365 million. Assuming that you will either win the Jackpot or the \$1 million prize, what's your expected value of winning?

Mega Millions is a similar lottery where you pick 5 balls out of 56 and a powerball from 46. Show that the odds of winning Mega Millions are lower than the Powerball lottery. On March 30, 2012, the Jackpot reached \$656 million. Is your expected value higher or lower than that calculated for the Powerball lottery?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) **Odds of winning the Powerball Jackpot**

To win the Powerball Jackpot, you must select all 5 numbers correctly (from 1 to 59, order doesn't matter) and the Powerball number (from 1 to 35).

- Number of ways to choose 5 numbers from 59:  
  $$
  \text{Combinations} = \binom{59}{5} = \frac{59!}{5! \cdot 54!} = 5{,}006{,}386
  $$
- Number of ways to choose the Powerball: 35

- Total number of possible tickets:  
  $$
  5{,}006{,}386 \times 35 = 175{,}223{,}510
  $$

- Probability of winning the Jackpot:  
  $$
  \frac{1}{175{,}223{,}510}
  $$

b) **Odds of winning the \$1 million**

To win \$1 million, you must select all 5 numbers correctly (from 1 to 59), but NOT the Powerball number.

- Number of ways to choose 5 numbers from 59: $5{,}006{,}386$
- Number of ways to NOT choose the Powerball: 34 (since there are 35 possible Powerballs, and you must miss the correct one)

- Total number of possible tickets: $5{,}006{,}386 \times 35 = 175{,}223{,}510$

- Number of winning tickets for \$1 million: $1 \times 34 = 34$

- Probability of winning \$1 million:
  $$
  \frac{34}{175{,}223{,}510} = \frac{1}{5{,}153{,}632}
  $$

c) **Expected value of winning (Jackpot = \$365 million, \$1 million prize)**

Let $E$ be the expected value:

- Probability of Jackpot: $1/175{,}223{,}510$
- Probability of \$1 million: $1/5{,}153{,}632$
- Assume you can only win one or the other, not both.

$$
E = \left(\frac{1}{175{,}223{,}510}\right) \times 365{,}000{,}000 + \left(\frac{1}{5{,}153{,}632}\right) \times 1{,}000{,}000
$$

Calculate each term:

- Jackpot: $\frac{365{,}000{,}000}{175{,}223{,}510} \approx \$2.08$
- \$1 million: $\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{5{,}153{,}632} \approx \$0.19$

So,
$$
E \approx \$2.08 + \$0.19 = \$2.27
$$

d) **Mega Millions odds**

- Pick 5 balls out of 56: $\binom{56}{5} = 3{,}819{,}816$
- Pick 1 powerball out of 46: $46$

- Total possible tickets: $3{,}819{,}816 \times 46 = 175{,}711{,}536$

- Probability of winning Mega Millions: $1/175{,}711{,}536$

- This is slightly *worse* odds than Powerball ($1/175{,}223{,}510$), so the odds of winning Mega Millions are actually *lower* (i.e., it's harder to win) than Powerball.

e) **Expected value for Mega Millions (\$656 million jackpot)**

- Probability of winning: $1/175{,}711{,}536$
- Expected value: $\frac{656{,}000{,}000}{175{,}711{,}536} \approx \$3.73$

So, the expected value for Mega Millions is higher than for Powerball, mainly due to the larger jackpot, even though the odds are slightly worse.


:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Joint Probability

A market research survey finds that in a particular week, $28\%$ of all adults watch a financial news television program; $17\%$ read a financial publication, and $13\%$ do both.

a) Fill in the blanks in the following joint probability table

|              | Watches TV | Doesn't Watch | Total |
| :----------- | :--------- | :------------ | :---- |
| Reads        | .13        |               | .17   |
| Doesn't Read |            |               |       |
|              | .28        |               | 1.00  |


b) What is the probability that someone who watches a financial TV program read a publication oriented towards finance?
c) What is the probability that someone who reads a finance publication watches a financial TV program.
d) Why aren't the answers to the above questions equal?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) All probabilities come from the given probabilities and the fact that the sum of the column/row probabilities must add to 1.

|              | Watches TV | Doesn't Watch | Total |
| :----------- | :--------- | :------------ | :---- |
| Reads        | .13        | .04           | .17   |
| Doesn't Read | .15        | .68           | .83   |
|              | .28        | .72           | 1.00  |

b) $$P(reads\mid TV)=P(reads \text{ and } TV)/P(TV)=.13/.28=.4643$$
c) $$P(TV\mid reads) = P(reads \text{ and } TV)/P(reads)=.13/.17=.7647$$

d) The reason for the difference is the denominators of the equations
    are different. This is an example of a base rate issue, it is more
    likely that someone who reads watches TV because fewer people read.
    This is not a condition of independence.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Conditional Probability

A local bank is reviewing its credit card policy. In the past 5% of card holders have defaulted. The bank further found that the chance of missing one or more monthly payments is 0.20 for customers who do not default. Of course, the probability of missing one or more payments for those who default is 1.

a) Given that a customer has missed a monthly payment, compute the
    probability that the customer will default.
a) The bank would like to recall its card if the probability that a
    customer will default is greater than 0.20. Should the bank recall
    its card if the customer misses a monthly payment? Why or why not?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

Let $D$ denote the event that a customer defaults and $M$ the event that a customer misses one or more monthly payments. We are given
$$
P(D) = 0.05, \quad P(M \mid D) = 1, \quad P(M \mid \bar{D}) = 0.20.
$$

a) By Bayes' rule,
$$
P(D \mid M) = \frac{P(M\mid D)P(D)}{P(M \mid D)P(D) + P(M\mid \bar{D}) P(\bar{D})} = \frac{(1)(0.05)}{(1)(0.05)+(0.20)(0.95)} = \frac{0.05}{0.24} = 0.2083.
$$
```{r}
PD <- 0.05; PnotD <- 1 - PD
PM_D <- 1; PM_notD <- 0.20
PM <- PM_D*PD + PM_notD*PnotD
PD_M <- PM_D*PD/PM
PD_M
```

a) Yes. Once a missed payment is observed, the posterior probability of default rises from the base rate of $5$% to about $20.8$%, which exceeds the bank's $20$% recall threshold. So the bank should recall the card whenever a customer misses a monthly payment.
:::
:::

## Correlation

The following table shows the descriptive statistics from $1000$ days of
returns on IBM and Exxon's stock prices.

                N   Mean    StDev    SE Mean
    IBM      1000   0.0009   0.0157  0.00049 
    Exxon    1000   0.0018   0.0224  0.00071

Here is the covariance table

              IBM     Exxon
    IBM     0.000247
    Exxon   0.000068  0.00050

a) What is the variance of IBM returns?
a) What is the correlation between IBM and Exxon's returns?
a) Consider a portfolio that invests $50$% in IBM and $50$% in Exxon.
    What are the mean and variance of the portfolio? Do you prefer this
    portfolio to just investing in IBM on its own?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) $$\sigma^2_{IBM}=0.000247$$
a) $$\rho=\frac{Cov(IBM,Exxon)}{\sigma_{IBM}\sigma_{Exxon}}=\frac{0.000068}{\sqrt{0.000247}\sqrt{0.00050}}=0.1935$$
a) $$\mu_p=w_{I}\mu_{I}+w_{E}\mu_{E}=(0.5)(0.0009)+(0.5)(0.0018)=0.00135$$
    $$\sigma^2_p=w_{I}^2\sigma_{I}^2+w_E^2\sigma_{E}^2+2w_Iw_E Cov(I,E)$$
    $$=(0.5)^2(0.000247)+(0.5)^2(0.00050)+2(0.5)(0.5)(0.000068)=0.000221$$
    Yes, because the portfolio has a higher mean return but with a lower

::: {#exr-}
## Normal Distribution

After Facebook's earnings announcement, we have the following distribution of returns. First, the stock beats earnings expectations $75$% of the time, and the other $25$% of the time, earnings are in line or disappoint. Second, when the stock beats earnings, the probability distribution of percent changes is normal with a mean of $10$% with a standard deviation of $5$% and, when the stock misses earnings, a normal with a mean of $-5$% and a standard deviation of $8$%, respectively.

a) Ahead of the earnings announcement, what is the probability that Facebook stock will have a return greater than $5$%?
a) Do you get the same answer for the probability that it drops by at least $5$%?
a) Use simulation to provide empirical answers with a sample of size N = 10,000, check and see how close you get to the theoretical answers you've found to the questions posed above. Provide histograms of the distributions you simulate.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

We have the following information:
$$
P(\textrm{Beat Earnings}) = 0.75 ~ \mathrm{ and} ~ P(\textrm{Not Beat Earnings}) = 0.25
$$ 
together with the following probabilities distributions
$$
R_{Beat}\sim N(0.10,0.05^2) ~ \mathrm{ and} ~ R_{Not}\sim N(-0.05,0.08^2)
$$ 
We want to find the probability that Facebook stock will have a return greater than 5%: 
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\textrm{Beat}) & \times P(R_{Beat}>0.05) + P(\textrm{Not}) \times P(R_{Not}>0.05)\\
&=0.75 \times (1-F_{Beat}(0.05)) + 0.25 \times (1-F_{Not}(0.05))
\end{aligned}
$$

```{r}
0.75*(1-pnorm(0.05,0.1,0.05)) + 0.25*(1-pnorm(0.05,-0.05,0.08)) #0.657
```

Therefore, the probability that Facebook stock beats a 5\% return is 65.7\%.

Similarly, for dropping at least 5\%, we want: 
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\textrm{Beat})\times P(R_{Beat}<-0.05) + P(\textrm{Not}) \times P(R_{Not}<-0.05)\\
=0.75 \times (F_{Beat}(-0.05)) + 0.25 \times (F_{Not}(-0.05))
\end{aligned}
$$
We can compute this is in R by the following commands:
  
```{r}
0.75*pnorm(-0.05,0.1,0.05) + 0.25*pnorm(-0.05,-0.05,0.08) #0.1260124
```
Therefore, the probability that Facebook stock drops at least 5\% is
12.6\%.\

:::
:::

## Probability
Answer the following statements TRUE or FALSE, providing a succinct explanation of your reasoning.

a) If the odds in favor of $A$ are 3:5 then $\mbox{P}(A) = 0.4$.
a) You roll two fair three-sided dice. The probability the two dice
    show the same number is 1/4.
a) If events $A$ and $B$ are independent and $\mbox{P}(A) > 0$ and
    $\mbox{P}(B)>0$, then $\mbox{P}(A \mbox{ and } B) > 0$.
a) If $\mbox{P}(A \; \text{ and} \;  B) \geq 0.5$ then $P(A) \leq 0.5$.
a) If two random variables have non-zero correlation, then they must be
    dependent.
a) If two random variables have zero correlation, then they must be
    independent.
a) If two random variables are independent, then the correlation
    between them must be zero.
a) If $P(A \text{ and } B) \leq 0.2$, then $P(A) \leq 0.2$.


::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) If the odds in favor of $A$ are 3:5 then $\mbox{P}(A) = 0.4$. FALSE $P(A) = \frac{3}{3+5} = 0.375$
a) You roll two fair three-sided dice. The probability the two dice show the same number is 1/4. FALSE $P = \frac{1}{3}\times\frac{1}{3}\times 3 = \frac{1}{3}$.
a) If events $A$ and $B$ are independent and $\mbox{P}(A) > 0$ and $\mbox{P}(B)>0$, then $\mbox{P}(A \mbox{ and } B) > 0$. TRUE $\mbox{P}(A \mbox{ and } B) = \mbox{P}(A) \times \mbox{P}(B)>0$.
a) If $\mbox{P}(A \; \text{ and} \;  B) \geq 0.5$ then $P(A) \leq 0.5$. FALSE Suppose A B are independent and $P(A) = 1$, $P(B) = 0.5$. $\mbox{P}(A \; \text{ and} \;  B) \geq 0.5$
a) If two random variables have non-zero correlation, then they must be dependent. TRUE If two random variables are independent, they always have 0 correlation. Therefore if correlation is not 0, they cannot be independent.
a) If two random variables have zero correlation, then they must be independent. FALSE Suppose $X$ takes value in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ with probability $\frac{1}{3}$ for each. $Y = X^2$, we have

$$
X = \begin{cases}
-1 & \text{with prob } 1/3\\
0  & \text{with prob } 1/3\\
1 & \text{with prob } 1/3
\end{cases},
Y = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{with prob } 2/3\\
0  & \text{with prob } 1/3\
\end{cases}
$$ 

It's easy to find that $\text{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$. But $Y$ is a function of $X$, so they are not independent.

a) If two random variables are independent, then the correlation between them must be zero. TRUE Independence implies uncorrelation, thus correlation is 0.
a) False, We only know $P(A \text{ and } B) \leq P(A)$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Binomial Distribution

The Downhill Manufacturing company produces snowboards. The average life of their product is $10$ years. A snowboard is considered defective if its life is less than $5$ years. The distribution is approximately normal with a standard deviation for the life of a board of $3$ years.

a) What's the probability of a snowboard being defective?
a) In a shipment of $120$ snowboards, what is the probability that the number of defective boards is greater than $10$?
a) Use simulation to provide empirical answers with a sample of size N = 10,000, check and see how close you get to the theoretical answers you've found to the questions posed above. Provide histograms of the distributions you simulate.

You can use R and simulation with `rbinom`, `rnorm` as an alternative


::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

Here we are given the following information: $L\sim N(10,3^2)$. We want to find the probability of a snowboard being defective:
$$
P(L<5)=F_L(5).
$$ 
This is simply the cumulative distribution function. We can find the solution by using the following R commands:
```{r}
pnorm(5,mean=10,sd=3) #0.04779035
```

Thus, the probability a snowboard is considered defective is 4.78%. Out of a shipment of 120 snowboards, the distribution of the number of defective boards is a Binomial Distribution parameterized as follows:
$$
N_{def}\sim Bin(120,0.0478).
$$ 
We want to find the probability:
$$
P(N_{def}>10)
$$
```{r}
pbinom(10,120,0.0478,lower.tail = FALSE) #0.02914742
```

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Chinese Stock Market

On August 24th, 2015, Chinese equities ended down $- 8.5$% (Black Monday). In the last $25$ years, the average is $0.09$% with a volatility of $2.6$%, and $56$% time close within one standard deviation. SP500, average is $0.03$% with a volatility of $1.1$%. $74$% time close within one standard deviation


![Economist article, August 2015.](fig/stock-monday.png){width="30%"}

Assuming a normal model for daily returns in each market:

a) Using the $25$-year mean and volatility for China, compute the $z$-score of the August 24, 2015, return and the probability of a daily decline at least as extreme as $-8.5$%.
a) Under a normal model, what fraction of days should a return fall within one standard deviation of the mean? Compare this theoretical fraction to the $56$% observed for China and the $74$% observed for the S&P 500.
a) Based on (a) and (b), what do these numbers suggest about how well a normal model describes Chinese equity returns compared to the S&P 500?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) Let $R \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with $\mu = 0.09$% and $\sigma = 2.6$%. The $z$-score of the $-8.5$% observation is
$$
z = \frac{-8.5 - 0.09}{2.6} = -3.30.
$$
```{r}
z <- (-8.5 - 0.09)/2.6
z
pnorm(z)
```
A decline this large is about $3.3$ standard deviations below the mean, and under the normal model has probability $P(R \le -8.5\%) \approx 0.00048$, or roughly $1$ in $2{,}097$ trading days (about once every $8$ years, assuming $252$ trading days per year).

a) For any normal random variable, $P(\mu-\sigma < R < \mu+\sigma) = \Phi(1)-\Phi(-1) \approx 0.683$, so $68.3$% of days should fall within one standard deviation under normality.
```{r}
pnorm(1) - pnorm(-1)
```
China's observed frequency ($56$%) is well below this theoretical value, while the S&P $500$'s ($74$%) is somewhat above it.

a) Neither market matches the normal model exactly, but the mismatch is far more dramatic for China: a smaller share of days cluster within one standard deviation of the mean, and (as Black Monday shows) extreme moves occur much more often than a Gaussian model predicts. This is the signature of a fat-tailed (leptokurtic) return distribution. The $-8.5$% crash, essentially "impossible" under the fitted normal model ($p\approx 0.0005$), is a symptom of this fat-tailed behavior rather than evidence that the mean and volatility were mis-estimated. The S&P $500$'s $74$%, being closer to (if still somewhat above) the $68.3$% benchmark, indicates its daily returns are comparatively better approximated by a normal distribution, though still not perfectly so.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Body Weight

Suppose that your model for weight $X$: Normal distribution with mean $190$ lbs and variance $100$ lbs. The problem is to identify the proportion of people have weights over 200 lbs?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

We are given that $\mu = 190$ and $\sigma^2 = 100$ so $\sigma = 10$. Our probability model is $X \sim N ( 190 , 100 )$.

$X$, to get $$Z = \frac{ X - \mu}{ \sigma } = \frac{ X - 190 }{ 10}$$

Now we compute the desired probability 
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(X>200) & = P \left ( \frac{ X - 190 }{ 10 } > \frac{ 200 - 190 }{10 } \right ) \\
& = P \left ( Z > 1 \right ).
\end{aligned}
$$ 
Now use the cdf function ($F_Z$) to get $$P ( Z > 1 ) = 1 - F_Z ( 1 ) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587$$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Google Returns

Suppose daily percentage returns for Google stock, $r$ (in percent), have sample mean $\bar r = 0.025$ and sample standard deviation $s = 1.1$, estimated from historical data. Assume returns are normally distributed, $r \sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, with $\mu$ and $\sigma$ estimated by $\bar r$ and $s$.

a) What is the probability of losing at least $3$% in a single day, that is, $P(r<-3)$?
a) What is the probability of gaining at least $3$% in a single day, that is, $P(r>3)$? Why does it differ from part (a), and why is the difference so small?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

Plugging in $\hat\mu = \bar r = 0.025$ and $\hat\sigma = s = 1.1$, we standardize.

a)
$$
P(r<-3) = P\left(Z< \frac{-3-0.025}{1.1}\right) = P(Z< -2.75).
$$
```{r}
pnorm(-3, mean = 0.025, sd = 1.1)
```
So $P(r<-3)\approx 0.003$, about a $0.3$% chance of losing $3$% or more on a given day.

a)
$$
P(r>3) = P\left(Z>\frac{3-0.025}{1.1}\right) = P(Z> 2.70).
$$
```{r}
1 - pnorm(3, mean = 0.025, sd = 1.1)
```
So $P(r>3)\approx 0.0034$. The two probabilities would be identical if $\mu=0$; the small asymmetry comes from the slightly positive mean $\bar r = 0.025$, which shifts a bit of probability mass from the left tail to the right tail. Because $\sigma = 1.1$ is so much larger than $\mu$, this asymmetry is barely noticeable in practice.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Portfolio Means, Standard Deviations and Correlation

Suppose you have a portfolio that is invested with a weight of 75% in the U.S. and 25% in HK. You take a sample of 10 years, or 120 months, of historical means, standard deviations, and correlations for U.S. and Hong Kong stock market returns. Given this information, compute the mean and standard deviation of the returns on your portfolio.

            N     MEAN    STDEV      
----------- ----- -------- -------- -- --
Hong Kong    120   0.0170   0.0751     
US           120   0.0115   0.0330     

Correlation = 0.3

Hint: you will find the following formulas useful. Let $R_p$ denote the return on your portfolio, which is a weighted combination $R_p = pX + (1 - p)Y$. Then 
$$
E(R_p) = p\mu_X + (1 - p)\mu_Y
$$
$$
Var(R_p) = p^2\sigma_X^2 + (1 - p)^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2p(1-p)\rho \sigma_X \sigma_Y
$$
where $\mu_X$, $\mu_Y$ and $\sigma_X$, $\sigma_Y$ are the underlying means and standard deviations for $X$ and $Y$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

Let $X$ denote US returns and $Y$ denote HK returns, with weight $p=0.75$ on the US and $1-p=0.25$ on HK, so $R_p = 0.75X + 0.25Y$. From the table, $\mu_X = 0.0115$, $\sigma_X = 0.0330$, $\mu_Y = 0.0170$, $\sigma_Y = 0.0751$, and $\rho = 0.3$.

Mean:
$$
E(R_p) = 0.75(0.0115) + 0.25(0.0170) = 0.008625 + 0.00425 = 0.012875,
$$
that is $1.29$% per month.

Variance:
$$
\begin{aligned}
Var(R_p) &= (0.75)^2 (0.0330)^2 + (0.25)^2(0.0751)^2 + 2(0.75)(0.25)(0.3)(0.0330)(0.0751)\\
&= 0.000613 + 0.000353 + 0.000278\\
&= 0.001244,
\end{aligned}
$$
so $\sigma(R_p) = \sqrt{0.001244} = 0.0353$, that is about $3.53$% per month.

```{r}
p <- 0.75
mu_us <- 0.0115; sd_us <- 0.0330
mu_hk <- 0.0170; sd_hk <- 0.0751
rho <- 0.3
mu_p <- p*mu_us + (1-p)*mu_hk
var_p <- p^2*sd_us^2 + (1-p)^2*sd_hk^2 + 2*p*(1-p)*rho*sd_us*sd_hk
sd_p <- sqrt(var_p)
c(mean = mu_p, var = var_p, sd = sd_p)
```

The portfolio's mean return ($1.29$%) sits between the US ($1.15$%) and HK ($1.70$%) means, as expected for a weighted average. Its standard deviation ($3.53$%) is below the weighted average of the two standard deviations ($0.75\times 3.30 + 0.25\times 7.51 = 4.35$%), which illustrates the diversification benefit of combining two assets that are not perfectly correlated ($\rho = 0.3$).
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Binomial
In the game Chuck-a-Luck, you pick a number from 1 to 6. You roll three dice. If your number doesn't appear on any dice, you lose \$1. If your number appears exactly once, you win \$1. If your number appears on exactly two dice, you win \$2. If your number appears on all three dice, you win \$3.

Hence, every outcome has how much you win or lose on the game, namely $-1, 1, 2$, or $3$.

a) Fill in the blanks in the pdf and cdf values

|      |     |     |     |     |
| :--- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |  
| X    | -1  | 1   | 2   | 3   |
| P(X) |     |     |     |     |
| F(X) |     |     |     |     |

Explain your reasoning carefully.

b) Compute the expected value of the game, $E(X)$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) PDF: This is a binomial experiment with n=3 and p=1/6. Plugging in
    for $x=0$: $$P(x=0)=(5/6)^3=.5787$$
    $$P(x=1)=3 (1/6)^1 \times (5/6)^2=.3472$$
    $$P(x=2)=3 (1/6)^2 \times (5/6)^1=.0694$$ $$P(x=3)=(1/6)^3=.0046$$
a) CDF: The values for this are the probabilities that X is less than
    or equal to a given value: $$F(x=0)=P(x \leq 0)=.5787$$
    $$F(x=1)=P(x \leq 1)=P(x=0)+P(x=1)=.9259$$ $$F(x=2)=.9954$$
    $$F(x=3)=1$$

The expected value is
$$
\sum_x x P_X ( x) = -1 \times 0.5787+1 \times 0.3472+2 \times 0.0694+3 \times 0.0046=-\$.08.
$$
You expect to lose 8 cents per game.

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Binomial Distribution
A real estate firm in Florida offers a free trip to Florida for potential customers. Experience has shown that of the people who accept the free trip, 5% decide to buy a property. If the firm brings $1000$ people, what is the probability that at least $125$ will decide to buy a property?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

In order to find the probability that *at least* $125$ decide to buy, the binomial distribution would require calculating the probabilities for 125-1000. Instead, we use the normal approximation for the binomial.
$$
\mu = np =50.
$$
$$
\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{1000\times .05\times .95}=\sqrt{47.5}=6.89
$$

Calculating the Z-score for 125: $Z=\frac{125-50}{6.89}=10.9.$ and $P(Z \geq 10.9)=0$.

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Expectation and Strategy

An oil company wants to drill in a new location. A preliminary geological study suggests that there is a $20$% chance of finding a small amount of oil, a $50$% chance of a moderate amount, and a $30$% chance of a large amount of oil. The company has a choice of either a standard drill that simply burrows deep into the earth or a more sophisticated drill that is capable of horizontal drilling and can therefore extract more, but is far more expensive. The following table provides the payoff table in millions of dollars under different states of the world and drilling conditions

           Oil           small   moderate   large
  --------------------- ------- ---------- -------
    Standard Drilling     20        30       40
   Horizontal Drilling    -20       40       80

Find the following

a) The mean and variance of the payoffs for the two different strategies
b) The strategy that maximizes their expected payoff
c) Briefly discuss how the variance of the payoffs would affect your decision if you were risk averse
d) How much are you willing to pay for a geological evaluation that would tell you with certainty the quantity of oil at the site prior to drilling?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) Using the plug-in rule, we get 
$$
\begin{aligned}
E(Standard) & = & 31\\
E(Horizontal) & = & 40\\
Var(Standard) & = & E(X^{2})-\left[E(X)\right]^{2}\\
& = & 1010-961\\
& = & 49\\
Var(Horizontal) & = & E(X^{2})-\left[E(X)\right]^{2}\\
& = & 2800-1600\\
& = & 1200
\end{aligned}
$$
```{r}
S = c(20,30,40)
P = c(0.2,0.5,0.3)
E_standard = sum(S*P)
H = c(-20,40,80)
E_horizontal = sum(H*P)
E_standard
E_horizontal
sum(S^2*P) - E_standard^2
sum(H^2*P) - E_horizontal^2
```
b) Given our analysis, horizontal drilling maximizes the expected payoff.
c) The strategy with higher expected payoff has a substantially higher variance. A risk averse person will settle for a strategy with lower expected payoff and lower variance, i.e., standard drilling, while a risk seeking person will choose horizontal drilling.
d) If the geological evaluation tells us with certainty the type of oil, then we will be able to chose the strategy which maximizes our payoff under different types of oil. Thus, the amount one should be willing to pay is the expected payoff under this revised schedule of payoff minus the maximum payoff under the current schedule. Given this
$$
WTP=0.2\times20+0.5\times40+0.3\times80-40=48-40=8
$$

Therefore, once should be willing to pay $\$8$ million for this information.

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Google Survey
Visitors to your website are asked to answer a single survey [Google
website](http://www.google.com) question before they get access to the
content on the page. Among all of the users, there are two categories

a) Random Clicker (RC)
a) Truthful Clicker (TC)


There are two possible answers to the survey: yes and no.

Random clickers would click either one with equal probability. You are also giving the information that the expected fraction of random clickers is $0.3$.

After a trial period, you get the following survey results. $65$% said Yes and $35$% said No.

How many people who are truthful clickers answered yes?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**: 

Given the information that the expected fraction of random clickers is 0.3, $$P(RC) = 0.3 \mbox{ and } P(TC) = 0.7$$ Conditioning on a random clickers, he would click either one with equal probability. 
$$
P(Yes \mid RC) = P(No \mid RC) = 0.5
$$ 
By the survey results, we know the proportion response of "Yes\" and "No\". 
$$
P(Yes) = 0.65 \mbox{ and } P(No) = 0.35
$$ 
Therefore, the probability that a truthful clicker answer "Yes\" is, 
$$
\begin{aligned}         
P(Yes \mid TC) &=& \frac{P(Yes)-P(Yes \mid RC)*P(RC)}{P(TC)} \\         
&=& \frac{0.65 - 0.5*0.3}{0.7} = 0.71     
\end{aligned}
$$ 
Notice that, we use law of total probability in the first equation.

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Homicide Rate (Poisson Distribution)

Suppose that there are $1.5$ homicides a week. This is the rate, so
$\lambda=1.5$. The Poisson model tells us that there is still a $1.4$% chance of
seeing $5$ homicides in a week
$$
p( X= 5 ) = \frac{e^{ - 1.5 } ( 1.5 )^5 }{5!} = 0.014
$$ 
On average, this will happen once every $71$ weeks, nearly once a year.

What's the chance of having zero homicides in a week?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

From the probability distribution we calculate
$$
p( X= 0 ) = \frac{e^{ - 1.5 } ( 1.5 )^0 }{0!} = 0.22
$$ 
In `R`
```{r}
dpois(0, 1.5)
```

So the probability is 22% You shouldn't be surprised to see this happening.

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Convolution of Exponentials
Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent and identically distributed as a $Exp(1)$ distribution. Their joint distribution is given by

$$
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \exp(-x)\exp(-y) \mathrm{ , where} \; \; 0 < x,y < \infty
$$

a) Use the convolution formula to find the distribution of     $X + \frac{1}{2} Y$.  Check your answer by also using a moment generating function     approach.
a) Guess what happens if you consider     $X + \frac{1}{2} Y + \frac{1}{3} Z$ where $Z$ is also $Exp(1)$?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

First, we need to show the family of exponential distributions is closed under scaling. Let $Z = aY$ so that $$P(Z \leq z) = P(Y \leq z/a) = 1 - \exp(-z/a)$$ Therefore, $Z \sim Exp(1/a)$ and $f_{aY} = \frac{1}{a}\exp(-Y/a)$.

Let $W = X + \frac{1}{2}Y$. Since $\frac{1}{2}Y \sim Exp(2)$ with density $2\exp(-2y)$, independent of $X$, the density of $W$ is the convolution
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_W(w) &= \int_0^w f_X(x) f_{\frac{1}{2}Y}(w-x)\,dx \\
&= \int_0^w \exp(-x)\cdot 2\exp(-2(w-x))\,dx \\
&= 2\exp(-2w)\int_0^w \exp(x)\,dx \\
&= 2\left(\exp(-w) - \exp(-2w)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

We can check this with moment generating functions. Since $X$ and $\frac{1}{2}Y$ are independent,
$$
M_W(t) = M_X(t)\cdot M_{\frac{1}{2}Y}(t) = \frac{1}{1-t}\cdot\frac{2}{2-t} = \frac{2}{(1-t)(2-t)}, \quad t<1.
$$
Integrating the density directly gives the same answer:
$$
M_W(t) = \int_0^\infty e^{tw}\cdot 2\left(e^{-w}-e^{-2w}\right)dw = \frac{2}{1-t} - \frac{2}{2-t} = \frac{2}{(1-t)(2-t)},
$$
confirming the convolution. Differentiating at $t=0$ gives $E(W) = M_W'(0) = 1 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2} = \E{X} + \frac{1}{2}\E{Y}$.

By the same argument, $W = X + \frac{1}{2} Y + \frac{1}{3} Z$ is a sum of independent exponentials with rates $1, 2, 3$, with density
$$
f_W(w) = 3e^{-w} - 6e^{-2w} + 3e^{-3w}.
$$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Normal

Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ are **independent** $N(0,1)$ random variables. Let $$Y_1 = X_1^2 + X_2^2, \quad Y_2 = \frac{X_1}{\sqrt{Y_1}}$$ 

a) Find joint distribution of $Y_1$ and $Y_2$. 
a) Are $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ independent or not? 
a) Can you interpret the result geometrically? 

Density of $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is $$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$$

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

Since $X_1, X_2$ are independent $N(0,1)$, their joint density is
$$
f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{2\pi} e^{-(x_1^2+x_2^2)/2}.
$$

*Jacobian.* The map $(x_1,x_2)\mapsto(y_1,y_2)$ with $y_1 = x_1^2+x_2^2$, $y_2 = x_1/\sqrt{y_1}$ is two-to-one: for fixed $(y_1,y_2)$ with $y_1>0$, $-1<y_2<1$, inverting gives
$$
x_1 = y_2\sqrt{y_1}, \qquad x_2 = \pm\sqrt{y_1(1-y_2^2)},
$$
i.e., the two points $(x_1,\pm x_2)$ both map to the same $(y_1,y_2)$. We compute the forward Jacobian and then account for both branches. Differentiating,
$$
\frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_1} = 2x_1, \qquad \frac{\partial y_1}{\partial x_2} = 2x_2,
$$
$$
\frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{y_1}} - \frac{x_1^2}{y_1^{3/2}} = \frac{1-y_2^2}{\sqrt{y_1}}, \qquad \frac{\partial y_2}{\partial x_2} = -\frac{x_1 x_2}{y_1^{3/2}}.
$$
So
$$
\begin{aligned}
J &= \det\begin{pmatrix} 2x_1 & 2x_2 \\ \dfrac{1-y_2^2}{\sqrt{y_1}} & -\dfrac{x_1x_2}{y_1^{3/2}} \end{pmatrix}
= -\frac{2x_1^2x_2}{y_1^{3/2}} - \frac{2x_2(1-y_2^2)}{\sqrt{y_1}} \\
&= -\frac{2x_2}{\sqrt{y_1}}\left(\frac{x_1^2}{y_1}+1-y_2^2\right) = -\frac{2x_2}{\sqrt{y_1}}\left(y_2^2+1-y_2^2\right) = -\frac{2x_2}{\sqrt{y_1}}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Using $|x_2| = \sqrt{y_1(1-y_2^2)}$, we get $|J| = 2\sqrt{1-y_2^2}$, so the inverse Jacobian is $1/|J| = 1/(2\sqrt{1-y_2^2})$. Since both branches $x_2 = \pm\sqrt{y_1(1-y_2^2)}$ give the same $y_1=x_1^2+x_2^2$ and hence the same value of $f_{X_1,X_2}$, we sum their (equal) contributions:
$$
f_{Y_1,Y_2}(y_1,y_2) = 2\times f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)\times\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-y_2^2}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-y_2^2}} e^{-y_1/2}, \qquad y_1>0,\ -1<y_2<1.
$$

a) The joint density found above factors as
$$
f_{Y_1,Y_2}(y_1,y_2) = \underbrace{\left[\tfrac12 e^{-y_1/2}\right]}_{f_{Y_1}(y_1)} \times \underbrace{\left[\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-y_2^2}}\right]}_{f_{Y_2}(y_2)}.
$$
So $Y_1 \sim \text{Exponential}(\text{rate}=1/2)$ (equivalently $\chi^2_2$), and $Y_2$ has the arcsine density on $(-1,1)$.

a) Because the joint density is exactly the product of the two marginals above, $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ are independent.

a) Write $(X_1,X_2) = R(\cos\Theta,\sin\Theta)$ in polar coordinates. Then $Y_1 = R^2$ is the squared distance from the origin, and $Y_2 = X_1/\sqrt{Y_1} = \cos\Theta$ is the cosine of the angle the point makes with the horizontal axis. The bivariate standard normal is rotationally symmetric (its density depends only on $x_1^2+x_2^2$), so the direction $\Theta$ is uniform on the circle and independent of the distance $R$ from the origin. Geometrically: how far a standard bivariate normal point lands from the origin carries no information about which direction it lands in, exactly the independence derived algebraically above.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 100000
X1 <- rnorm(n); X2 <- rnorm(n)
Y1 <- X1^2 + X2^2
Y2 <- X1/sqrt(Y1)
c(mean_Y1 = mean(Y1), var_Y1 = var(Y1))   # theory: mean = 2, var = 4
c(mean_Y2 = mean(Y2), var_Y2 = var(Y2))   # theory: mean = 0, var = 0.5
cor(Y1, Y2)                               # theory: 0 (independence)
```
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Tesla Supplier

Tesla purchases Lithium as a raw material for their batteries from either of two suppliers and is concerned about the amounts of impurity the material contains. The percentage impurity levels in consignments of the Lithium follows closely a normal distribution with the means and standard deviations given in the table below. The company is particularly anxious that the impurity level not exceed $5$% and wants to purchase from the supplier who is more likely to meet that specification.

                Mean   Standard Deviation
  ------------ ------ --------------------
   Supplier A   4.4           0.4
   Supplier B   4.2           0.6

a) Which supplier should be chosen?
a) What if Supplier B implements some quality control which has no effect on the standard deviation but raises their mean to $4.6$?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) We need to find the probability that the impurity level exceeds 5% for each supplier.
For Supplier A: $Z_A = \frac{5 - 4.4}{0.4} = 1.5$. $P(X > 5) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668$.
For Supplier B: $Z_B = \frac{5 - 4.2}{0.6} = 1.33$. $P(X > 5) = P(Z > 1.33) = 1 - 0.9082 = 0.0918$.
Supplier A has a lower probability of exceeding the impurity limit, so Supplier A should be chosen.

b) If Supplier B's mean shifts to 4.6 (with sd=0.6):
$Z_B = \frac{5 - 4.6}{0.6} = 0.67$. $P(X > 5) = P(Z > 0.67) = 1 - 0.7486 = 0.2514$.
This makes Supplier B even worse.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Berkshire Realty

Berkshire Realty is interested in determining how long a property stays
on the housing market. For a sample of $800$ homes, they find the
following probability table for the length of stay on the market before
being sold as a function of the asking price

  ----------------- ---------- ------- ---------
  Days until Sold    Under 20   20-40   over 40
  Under \$250K          50       40       10
  \$250-500K            20       150      80
  \$500-1M              20       280      100
  Over \$1 M            10       30       10
  ----------------- ---------- ------- ---------

a) What is the probability of a randomly selected house that is listed over $40$ days before being sold?
a) What is the probability that a randomly selected initial asking price is under $250$K?
a) What is the joint probability of both of the above events happening?
a) Assuming that a contract has just been signed to list a home for under \$500K, what is the probability that Berkshire realty will sell the home in under $40$ days?


::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) $P(\mbox{over 40}) = \frac{10+80+100+10}{800} = 25\%$
a) $P(\mbox{under 250K}) = \frac{50+40+10}{800} = 12.5\%$
a) $P(\mbox{over 40 and under 250K}) = \frac{10}{800} = 1.25\%$
a) $P(\mbox{under 40 and under 500K}) = \frac{50+40+20+150}{50+40+20+150+10+80} = 74.29\%$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## True/False

a) If $\mathbb{P} \left ( A \; \mathrm{ and} \; B \right ) \leq 0.2$ then $\mathbb{P} (A) \leq 0.2$.
a) If $P( A | B ) = 0.5$ and $P(B ) = 0.5$, then the events $A$ and $B$ are necessarily independent.
a) A box has three drawers; one contains two gold coins, one contains two silver coins, and one contains one gold and one silver coin. Assume that one drawer is selected randomly and that a randomly selected coin from that drawer turns out to be gold. Then the probability that the chosen drawer contains two gold coins is $50$%.
a) Suppose that $P(A) = 0.4 , P(B)=0.5$ and $P( A  \text{ or }B ) = 0.7$ then $P( A  \text{ and }B ) = 0.3$.
a) If $P( A  \text{ or }B ) = 0.5$ and $P(A  \text{ and }B ) = 0.5$, then $P(A) = P( B)$.
a) The following data on age and marital status of $140$ customers of a Bondi beach night club were taken

    | Age      | Single | Not Single |
    | :------- | :----- | :--------- |
    | Under 30 | 77     | 14         |
    | Over 30  | 28     | 21         |
    |          |        |            |

   Given these data, age and marital status are independent.
a) If $P( A  \text{ and }B ) = 0.5$ and $P(A) = 0.1$, then $P(B|A) = 0.1$.
a) In a group of students, $45$% play golf, $55$% play tennis, and $70$% play at least one of these sports. Then the probability that a student plays golf but not tennis is $15$%.
a) The following probability table relating age to marital status

    | Age      | Single | Not Single |
    | :------- | :----- | :--------- |
    | Under 30 | 0.55   | 0.10       |
    | Over 30  | 0.20   | 0.15       |
    |          |        |            |

   Given these probabilities, age and marital status are independent.
a) Thirty-six different kinds of ice cream can be found at Ben and Jerry's. There are $58{,}905$ different combinations of four choices of ice cream.
a) Suppose that for a certain Caribbean island, the probability of a hurricane is $0.25$, the probability of a tornado is $0.44$, and the probability of both occurring is $0.22$. Then the probability of a hurricane or a tornado occurring is $0.05$.
a) If $P ( A  \text{ and }B ) \geq 0.10$, then $P(A) \geq 0.10$.
a) If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events, then $P(A|B) = 0$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) False. We only know $\mathbb{P} \left ( A \; \mathrm{ and} \; B \right ) \leq \mathbb{P}(A)$.
a) False. This is not necessarily true. We need more information about each event to definitively say so.
a) False. Knowing that we have a gold coin, there is 2/3 chance of being in the 2 gold coin drawer and a 1/3 chance of being in the 1 gold coin drawer. Therefore, the probability that the chosen drawer contains two gold coins is 2/3.
a) False. $P(A \text{ and }B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \text{ or }B)=0.2$
a) True. We know that $P( A  \text{ or }B ) = P(A) +P(B) - P(A  \text{ and }B )$ and so $P(A) + P(B) =1$. Also $P( A) \geq P( A  \text{ and }B ) = 0.5$ and so $P(A)=P(B) = 0.5$
a) False. We can compute conditional probabilities as $P ( S \mid U_{30} ) = 0.8462 , P ( M \mid U_{30} ) = 0.1538$ and $P ( S \mid O_{30} ) = 0.5714 , P ( M \mid O_{30} ) = 0.4286$. The events aren't independent as the conditional probabilities are not the same.
a) False. $P(B \mid A) = P( A  \text{ and }B ) / P( A)$ would be greater than one
a) True. $P(G)=0.45, P(T)=0.55, P(G  \text{ or }T) = 0.70$ implies $P(G  \text{ and }\bar{T}) = 0.15$
a) False. $P ( X > 30  \text{ and }Y = \mathrm{ married} ) = 0.15 \neq 0.35 \times 0.25
=  P ( X > 30 )P( Y = \mathrm{ married} )$
a) True. Combinations are given by $36!/(36-4)!4! =58{,}905$
a) False. $P(H \text{ or }T)=P(H)+P(T)-P(H \text{ and }T)=0.25+0.44-0.22=0.47$
a) True. $A  \text{ and }B$ is a subset of $A$ and so $P(A) \geq P(A  \text{ and }B) = 0.10$
a) True. By definition, if $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive events then $P( A  \text{ and }B)=0$ and so $P(A \mid B) = P(A  \text{ and }B)/P(B) = 0$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Marginal and Joint

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent with a joint distribution given by $$f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{ \frac{1}{xy} }        \exp \left( - \frac{x}{2} - \frac{y}{2} \right)     \text{ where }  x, y > 0 .$$ Identify the following distributions

a) The marginal distribution of $X$
a) Compute the joint distribution of $U = X$ and $V = X+Y$
a) Compute the marginal distribution of $V$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) $$\begin{aligned}         \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{x y}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(x+y)} dy &=         \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} e^{-\frac{x}{2}}         \end{aligned}$$
a) We perform the substitutions $y \to v-x$ and $x \to u$ and obtain     the parameter vector $\begin{pmatrix}u \\ v-u\end{pmatrix}$, which     has the following Jacobian: $$\begin{aligned}         \left|\begin{pmatrix}         1 & 0 \\         -1 & 1          \end{pmatrix}\right| = 1         \end{aligned}$$ Thus, the transformed distribution is     $$\begin{aligned}         f_{U,V}(u,v) &= \frac{1}{2 \pi} \frac{1}{\sqrt{u(v-u)}} e^{-v/2}         \end{aligned}$$
a) $$\begin{aligned}         \frac{1}{2 \pi} \int_0^v \frac{1}{\sqrt{u(v-u)}} e^{-v/2} du &=          \frac{1}{2} e^{-v/2}         \end{aligned}$$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Conditional

a) Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent standard $N(0,1)$ random variables.     Then $X^2 + Y^2$ is an exponential distribution.
a) Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent Poisson random variables with rates     $\lambda$ and $\mu$, respectively. Show that the conditional distribution of $X | (X+Y)$ is Binomial with $n = X+Y$ and     $p = \lambda / ( \lambda + \mu)$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) True. The random variable $(X^2+Y^2)$ has a $\chi^2_2$ distribution,     and this is an exponential distribution with $\lambda=1/2$.
a) $$P(X=l \mid X+Y =n) = \frac{P(X=l , X+Y=n)}{P(X+Y=n)} = \frac{P(X=l, Y= n-l)}{P(X+Y=n)}$$     $$=\frac{P(X=l)P(Y=n-l)}{P(X+Y=n)}=\frac{(e^{-\lambda}\lambda^l/l!)(e^{-\mu}\mu^{n-l}/(n-l)!)}{e^{-\lambda-\mu}(\lambda+\mu)^n/n!}=\frac{n!}{l!(n-l)!}\frac{\lambda^l\mu^{n-l}}{(\lambda+\mu)^n}$$     $$=p^l (1-p)^{n-l}\frac{n!}{l!(n-l)!}$$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Joint and Marginal

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent exponential random variables with means $\lambda$ and $\mu$, respectively.

a) Find the joint distribution of $U = X+Y$ and $V = X / ( X+Y)$.
a) Find the marginal distributions for $U$ and $V$.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) The joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ is given by     $$f_{X,Y} ( x , y ) = \frac{1}{\lambda \mu} \exp \left ( - \frac{x}{\lambda}  - \frac{y}{\mu} \right )$$ The transformation $u =x+y$ and     $v= x / ( x+y)$ has inverse given by $x = uv$, $y = u ( 1 - v)$.     Hence, the Jacobian is $u$. The joint distribution of $(U,V)$ is     then     $$f_{U,V} ( u,v) =  \frac{u}{\lambda \mu} \exp \left ( - \frac{uv}{\lambda} - \frac{u(1-v)}{\mu} \right )$$
a) The marginal distribution of $U$ is given by
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_U(u)& = \int_0^1 f_{U,V} ( u,v) dv\\
&= \frac{1}{\lambda - \mu} \left ( \exp \left ( - \frac{ u}{ \lambda } \right )      -  \exp \left ( - \frac{ u}{ \mu } \right ) \right )
\end{aligned}
$$

The marginal distribution of $V$ is given by
$$
f_V ( v) = \int_{0}^{\infty} f_{U,V} ( u,v) du
$$
Hence,
$$
f_V(v) = \frac{ \lambda \mu }{ ( \mu v + \lambda ( 1-v) )^2 }
$$

:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Bivariate Normal Transformation

Let $X, Y$ have a bivariate normal density with density given by $$f_{X,Y} ( x, y) = \frac{1}{ 2 \pi \sqrt{ ( 1 - \rho^2 )} } \exp \left ( - \frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}  \left ( x^2 - 2 \rho x y + y^2 \right ) \right )$$ Consider the transformation $W=X$ and $Z = \frac{ Y - \rho X}{ \sqrt{ 1 - \rho^2 } }$. Show that $W , Z$ are independent and identify their distributions.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

The Jacobian of this linear transformation is given by $J = \sqrt{ 1 - \rho^2 }$. Knowing that $X = g(W,Z) = W$, and $Y = h(W,Z) = \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z + \rho W$, and Jacobian $J$, we can apply the transformation formula:
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{W,Z} (w,z) &=& f_{X,Y} (g(w,z),h(w,z)) |J|\\
&=& f_{X,Y} (w, \sqrt{1-\rho^2} Z + \rho W)\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\\
&=& \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp \left ( -\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)} \left ( w^2-2\rho w \left ( \sqrt{1-\rho^2} z + \rho w \right ) + \left ( \sqrt{1-\rho^2} z + \rho w \right )^2 \right ) \right )\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\\
&=& \frac{1}{2\pi} \exp\left ( -\frac{(1-\rho^2)(w^2+z^2)}{2(1-\rho^2)} \right )\\
&=& \frac{1}{2\pi} \exp\left ( -\frac{w^2+z^2}{2} \right )\\
&\propto& \exp \left ( -\frac{w^2}{2} \right ) \exp\left ( -\frac{z^2}{2} \right )\\
&\propto& f_W(w) f_Z(z)
\end{aligned}
$$
Because we can write the joint distribution of $(W,Z)$ as the product of two marginal distributions, $W$ and $Z$ are independent. $W$, $Z$ both follow a standard normal distribution with mean $0$ and variance $1$.

:::
:::
