::: {#exr-inverse-cdf-sampling}
## Sampling via the Inverse CDF Method

The chapter's inverse CDF method turns uniform draws into samples from any continuous distribution: if $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and $F$ is a continuous, strictly increasing CDF, then $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$. Here you build such a sampler from scratch and check it against R's built-in generators.

a) (Pen-and-Pencil) Let $X$ have CDF $F(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x \ge 0$ (the $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ distribution), with $\lambda = 2$. Solve $u = F(x)$ for $x$ to obtain the inverse CDF $F^{-1}(u)$ on $u \in (0,1)$. Then, using the fact that $F$ is strictly increasing, show that if $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ the variable $X = F^{-1}(U)$ satisfies $\prob{X \le x} = F(x)$, so that $X$ is genuinely $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$.

a) In R, write a function `sample_exp(n, lambda)` that draws $n$ i.i.d. $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ variates using only `runif()` and your formula from part (a). Do not call `rexp()` or `qexp()` inside it. Set a seed and generate $N = 10{,}000$ draws with $\lambda = 2$.

a) Compare the sample mean and variance of your draws to the theoretical $\E{X} = 1/\lambda$ and $\Var{X} = 1/\lambda^2$. Overlay a histogram of your draws on the theoretical $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ density (`dexp`), and produce a Q-Q plot of your sample against theoretical quantiles (`qexp` evaluated at `ppoints`).

a) Generate a second sample of size $N$ with R's built-in `rexp(N, rate = lambda)` and run a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (`ks.test`) comparing it to your inverse-CDF sample. What do you conclude about the two generators?

a) Now let $X$ have CDF $F(x) = x^2$ on $[0,1]$, with density $f(x) = 2x$. Derive $F^{-1}(u)$ by hand, adapt your sampler, generate $N = 10{,}000$ draws, and check the sample mean and variance against the theoretical $\E{X} = 2/3$ and $\Var{X} = 1/18$.

a) (Discussion) The chapter notes that for the Normal distribution $F^{-1}$ has no closed form, so only numerical inversion is available. Generate $10{,}000$ draws via `qnorm(runif(10000))` and compare their histogram to `rnorm(10000)`. Explain why this still counts as inverse CDF sampling even though no closed-form $F^{-1}$ was derived by hand in the style of part (a).

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a) Setting $u = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}$ and solving for $x$,
$$
e^{-\lambda x} = 1 - u \;\Longrightarrow\; -\lambda x = \log(1-u) \;\Longrightarrow\; x = F^{-1}(u) = -\frac{\log(1-u)}{\lambda}.
$$
Because $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, its inverse $F^{-1}$ is well defined and strictly increasing, so the events $\{F^{-1}(U) \le x\}$ and $\{U \le F(x)\}$ coincide. Hence, for any $x \ge 0$,
$$
\prob{X \le x} = \prob{F^{-1}(U) \le x} = \prob{U \le F(x)} = F(x),
$$
where the last step uses $\prob{U \le a} = a$ for $a = F(x) \in [0,1]$ when $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$. Thus $X = F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$, that is, it is $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$.

b) The sampler is a one-liner read straight off the formula in part (a):
```{r}
#| echo: true
sample_exp <- function(n, lambda) -log(1 - runif(n)) / lambda
set.seed(1)
lambda <- 2; N <- 10000
x <- sample_exp(N, lambda)
summary(x)
```

c) The sample moments match the theoretical values closely:
```{r}
#| echo: true
c(sample_mean = mean(x), sample_var = var(x),
  theory_mean = 1 / lambda, theory_var = 1 / lambda^2)
```
The sample mean $0.503$ and variance $0.250$ sit right on the theoretical $\E{X} = 1/\lambda = 0.5$ and $\Var{X} = 1/\lambda^2 = 0.25$. The histogram tracks the exponential density and the Q-Q plot falls on the $45$-degree line, confirming the draws follow $\text{Exponential}(2)$.
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "Sample histogram vs. Exponential(2) density"
#|   - "Q-Q plot against Exponential(2) quantiles"
hist(x, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "lightblue", main = "", xlab = "x")
curve(dexp(x, rate = lambda), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
qqplot(qexp(ppoints(N), rate = lambda), x, col = "grey40",
       xlab = "theoretical quantiles", ylab = "sample quantiles")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

d) Compare against R's built-in exponential generator with a two-sample test:
```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(2)
y <- rexp(N, rate = lambda)
ks.test(x, y)
```
The test statistic is tiny ($D = 0.007$) and the $p$-value is large ($\approx 0.97$), so we cannot reject the null that the two samples share a distribution. The hand-built inverse CDF sampler is statistically indistinguishable from `rexp`, up to Monte Carlo noise.

e) Solving $u = x^2$ on $[0,1]$ gives $F^{-1}(u) = \sqrt{u}$, so the sampler is `sqrt(runif(n))`:
```{r}
#| echo: true
sample_f <- function(n) sqrt(runif(n))
set.seed(3)
z <- sample_f(N)
c(sample_mean = mean(z), sample_var = var(z),
  theory_mean = 2 / 3, theory_var = 1 / 18)
```
The sample mean $0.664$ and variance $0.0562$ match the theoretical $\E{X} = 2/3 \approx 0.667$ and $\Var{X} = 1/18 \approx 0.0556$, so the method generalizes well beyond the exponential example.

f) The two constructions produce visually identical draws:
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "qnorm(runif(N)): inverse CDF draws"
#|   - "rnorm(N): built-in generator"
set.seed(4); xn <- qnorm(runif(N))
set.seed(5); rn <- rnorm(N)
hist(xn, breaks = 40, col = "lightblue", main = "", xlab = "x")
hist(rn, breaks = 40, col = "lightgreen", main = "", xlab = "x")
```
Both histograms are bell-shaped with mean near $0$ and standard deviation near $1$. This is still the inverse CDF method because `qnorm` is exactly R's numerical implementation of $\Phi^{-1}$: we apply $F^{-1}$ to a $\text{Uniform}(0,1)$ draw, just as in part (a). The only difference is that $\Phi^{-1}$ is evaluated by a numerical routine rather than a closed-form algebraic expression, precisely the distinction the chapter draws between the exponential (exact inversion) and normal (approximate inversion) cases. The same uniform-to-target logic underlies the Monte Carlo methods discussed in @sec-computational-bridge.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-lln-convergence}
## The Law of Large Numbers in Action

Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ be i.i.d. rolls of a fair six-sided die, so $X_i \in \{1,\ldots,6\}$ each with probability $1/6$. The population mean and variance are
$$
\mu = \E{X_i} = 3.5, \qquad \sigma^2 = \Var{X_i} = \frac{35}{12} \approx 2.9167.
$$
Let $\bar X_n = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ denote the running sample mean after $n$ rolls.

a) Set a seed and simulate $n=100{,}000$ die rolls. Compute the running sample mean $\bar X_n$ for every $n$ from $1$ to $100{,}000$ (the cumulative sum of the rolls divided by the running count, exactly as in the chapter's opening coin-flip figure) and plot it against $n$ on a log scale, together with a horizontal reference line at $\mu=3.5$. Repeat the simulation to generate $6$ independent sample paths and overlay them on one plot. Comment on what happens to the paths as $n$ grows.
a) For $n \in \{10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000\}$, estimate the standard deviation of $\bar X_n$ empirically: for each $n$, simulate $M=1000$ independent replications of $\bar X_n$ and compute their sample standard deviation. Compare this empirical standard deviation to the theoretical value $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and plot both against $n$ on a log-log scale. What is the slope of the resulting line, and what does it confirm about how the spread of the sample mean shrinks with $n$?
a) (Pen-and-Pencil) Using Chebyshev's inequality, $P(|\bar X_n - \mu| > \epsilon) \le \sigma^2/(n\epsilon^2)$, find the smallest $n$ that guarantees $P(|\bar X_n - 3.5|>0.1) \le 0.05$. How does this guaranteed $n$ compare to the sample sizes in part (b) at which the simulated spread of $\bar X_n$ is already comfortably small? What does this say about how conservative the Chebyshev bound is in practice?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

a)
```{r}
set.seed(1)
mu <- 3.5                     # true mean of a fair die roll
n <- 1e5                       # draws per path
K <- 6                        # number of independent sample paths
paths <- sapply(1:K, function(k) cumsum(sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE)) / (1:n))
matplot(paths, type = "l", lty = 1, col = 1:K, log = "x",
        xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = expression(bar(X)[n]),
        main = "Running sample mean of die rolls")
abline(h = mu, col = "red", lwd = 2)
paths[c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 1e5), 1]
```
For this seed, the first path's running mean is $3.000$ at $n=10$, $3.520$ at $n=100$, $3.514$ at $n=1000$, $3.5138$ at $n=10{,}000$, and $3.5055$ at $n=100{,}000$, tracking $\mu=3.5$ increasingly closely. All six paths wander widely for small $n$, then narrow and settle around the red reference line as $n$ grows into the thousands and beyond: exactly the behavior predicted by the law of large numbers. No individual path is guaranteed to hit $3.5$ exactly, but each is squeezed ever closer to it.

a)
```{r}
set.seed(2)
sigma <- sqrt(35/12)                     # true sd of a single die roll
n_grid <- c(10, 100, 1000, 10000, 100000)
M <- 1000                                # replications per sample size
emp_sd <- sapply(n_grid, function(n)
  sd(replicate(M, mean(sample(1:6, n, replace = TRUE)))))
data.frame(n = n_grid, empirical_sd = round(emp_sd, 5), theoretical_sd = round(sigma/sqrt(n_grid), 5))
```
```{r}
plot(n_grid, emp_sd, log = "xy", type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "sd of sample mean (log scale)",
     main = "Shrinkage of sd(Xbar_n) at rate 1/sqrt(n)")
lines(n_grid, sigma/sqrt(n_grid), col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("empirical", "theoretical"), col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1, pch = c(19, NA))
coef(lm(log(emp_sd) ~ log(n_grid)))[2]
```
Empirical and theoretical standard deviations agree closely at every $n$ (for example, $0.0542$ vs. $0.0540$ at $n=1000$, and $0.0054$ vs. $0.0054$ at $n=100{,}000$), and a line fit through the log-log points has slope $-0.498$, indistinguishable in practice from the $-1/2$ predicted by $\sd{\bar X_n} = \sigma/\sqrt n$. Each additional factor of $100$ in $n$ shrinks the spread of the sample mean by a factor of $10$.

a) Setting $\epsilon=0.1$ and the right-hand side to $0.05$,
$$
\frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2} \le 0.05 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n \ge \frac{\sigma^2}{0.05\,\epsilon^2} = \frac{35/12}{0.05 \times 0.01} = 5833.3,
$$
so Chebyshev only guarantees the desired accuracy once $n \ge 5834$. Yet part (b) shows the empirical spread is already tight at much smaller $n$: at $n=1000$ (fewer than a fifth of Chebyshev's requirement), $\sd{\bar X_n}\approx 0.054$, about half the tolerance $\epsilon=0.1$; at $n=10{,}000$, $\sd{\bar X_n}\approx 0.017$, less than a fifth of $\epsilon$. Chebyshev's bound has to hold for every distribution with the same mean and variance, however badly behaved, so it must be conservative. For this particular bounded, well-behaved random variable, the true concentration of $\bar X_n$ around $\mu$ is far tighter than the bound alone would suggest.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-port}
## Portfolio Means, Standard Deviations and Correlation
You want to build a portfolio of exchange traded funds (ETFs) for your retirement strategy. You're thinking of whether to invest in growth or value stocks, or maybe a combination of both. Vanguard has two ETFs, one for growth (VUG) and one for value (VTV).

a) Plot the historical price series for VUG vs VTV.
a) Calculate the means and standard deviations of both ETFs.
a) Calculate their covariance.
a) Suppose you decide on a portfolio that is a 50 / 50 split. Calculate
  the new mean and variance of your portfolio.
a) Which portfolio best suits you?
a) What's the probability that growth (VUG) will beat value (VTV) in
  the future?

You will find the following formulas useful. Let $P$ denote the return on your portfolio which is a weighted combination $P = aX + bY$. Then
$$
E(P) = aE(X) + bE(Y )
$$
$$
Var(P ) = a^2Var(X) + b^2Var(Y ) + 2abCov(X, Y ),
$$ 
where $Cov(X, Y )$ is the covariance for $X$ and $Y$.

*Hint:* You can use the following code to get the data
```{r eval=F}
#| echo: true
library(quantmod)
getSymbols(c("VUG","VTV"), from = "2015-01-01", to = "2024-01-01")
VUG = VUG$VUG.Adjusted
VTV = VTV$VTV.Adjusted
```

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(quantmod)
getSymbols(c("VUG","VTV"), from = "2015-01-01", to = "2024-01-01");
VUG = VUG$VUG.Adjusted
VTV = VTV$VTV.Adjusted
plot(VUG, type = "l", col = "red", main = "VUG")
plot(VTV, type = "l", col = "red", main = "VTV")
VUG = as.numeric(VUG)
VTV = as.numeric(VTV)
n=length(VUG)
VUG = VUG[2:n]/VUG[1:(n-1)]-1
VTV = VTV[2:n]/VTV[1:(n-1)]-1
mean(VUG)
mean(VTV)
sd(VUG)
sd(VTV)
cov(VUG, VTV)

# portfolio mean and variance
portfolio_mean_1 = 0.5 * mean(VUG) + 0.5 * mean(VTV)
portfolio_var_1 = 0.5^2 * var(VUG) + 0.5^2 * var(VTV) + 2 * 0.5 * 0.5 * cov(VUG, VTV)
portfolio_sd_1 = sqrt(portfolio_var_1)
```
You may say VUG or VTV best suits you, as long as you give an explanation such as you are risk aversion or not. Now we consider mean and variance of VUG - VTV,

```{r}
mean_1 = mean(VUG) - mean(VTV)
var_1 = var(VUG) + var(VTV) + 2 * 1 * (-1) * cov(VUG, VTV)
sd_1 = sqrt(var_1)
```
Therefore the probability that VUG - VTV $<0$ is
 
```{r}
pnorm(0, mean_1, sd = sd_1)
```

However, we care about the probability that VUG beats VTV, that is
$P(VUG > VTV) = P(VUG - VTV > 0) 
```{r}
pnorm(0, mean_1, sd = sd_1, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

:::

Use the `superbowl1.txt` and `derby2016.csv` datasets. The Superbowl contains data on the outcome of all previous Superbowls. For the Derby data.

```{r superbowl}
# import superbowl data

######################
# part 1
######################

# add a 45 degree line to compare

mean(y)

sd(y)

beta
```

::: {#exr-}
## Back Cast US Presidential Elections

Use data from presidential polls to predict the winner of the elections.
We will be using data from <http://www.electoral-vote.com/>. The goal is
to use simulations to predict the winning percentage for each of the
candidates. Use `election.Rmd` script as the starter.

Report the prediction as a 50% confidence interval for each of the
candidates.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

The approach uses simulation-based inference:

1. For each state, the poll gives an estimate $\hat{p}$ of the Democratic vote share with margin of error $m$. Model the true vote share as $p \sim N(\hat{p}, (m/1.96)^2)$.

2. Simulate $B = 10{,}000$ elections. In each simulation, draw $p_s$ for each state $s$, assign that state's electoral votes to the candidate with $p_s > 0.5$, and sum electoral votes.

3. The 50% confidence interval is the interval $[q_{0.25}, q_{0.75}]$ of the simulated electoral vote totals.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# See election.Rmd for data loading and state-level poll processing.
# The key simulation loop:
B <- 10000
ev_dem <- numeric(B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  p_sim <- rnorm(nrow(polls), polls$dem_pct, polls$moe / 1.96)
  wins <- p_sim > 0.5
  ev_dem[b] <- sum(polls$electoral_votes[wins])
}

cat("50% CI for Democratic EV:", quantile(ev_dem, c(0.25, 0.75)), "\n")
cat("P(Dem wins):", mean(ev_dem >= 270), "\n")
hist(ev_dem, breaks = 50, main = "Simulated Electoral Votes")
abline(v = 270, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Russian Parliament Election Fraud

On September 28, 2016 United Russia party won a super majority of seats, which will allow them to change the Constitution without any votes of other parties. Throughout the day, there were reports of voting fraud, including video purporting to show officials stuffing ballot boxes. Additionally, results in many regions demonstrate that United Russia on many poll stations got anomalously closed results, for example, 62.2% in more than hundred poll stations in Saratov Region.

Using the assumption that United Russia's range in Saratov was \[57.5%, 67.5%\] and results for each poll station are rounded to one decimal point (when measure in percent), calculate probability that in 100 poll stations out of 1800 in Saratov Region the majority party got exactly 62.2%.

Do you think it can happen by chance?

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

The range [57.5%, 67.5%] spans 10 percentage points. With rounding to one decimal, there are 101 possible values (57.5, 57.6, ..., 67.5). If poll station results are independent and uniformly distributed across this range, the probability of any single station reporting exactly 62.2% is $p = 1/101 \approx 0.0099$.

The number of stations reporting 62.2% out of 1800 follows a Binomial distribution: $X \sim \text{Binomial}(1800, 1/101)$.

The expected number is $\E{X} = 1800/101 \approx 17.8$. The probability that 100 or more stations report exactly 62.2% is:

```{r}
p <- 1/101
n <- 1800
k <- 100
prob <- 1 - pbinom(k - 1, n, p)
cat("P(X >= 100) =", prob, "\n")
cat("Expected count:", n * p, "\n")
```

The probability is essentially zero. Getting 100 identical results when we expect about 18 is astronomically unlikely under the assumption of independent, legitimate voting. This is strong statistical evidence of fraud.
:::
:::

::: {#exr-}
## Weather Data Analysis

Use the high-resolution data from the DCA Airport weather station (`weather_dca.csv` in the data folder), which contains sixteen years of roughly hourly observations.

A useful climate metric should help understand day-to-day life impacts, going beyond simple averages. Consider questions like:

- How often will I be biking to work in below-freezing temperatures?
- How many days a year will I see the sun?
- How many days do I need a raincoat during commute times?

a) Design a climate metric that you would find personally useful.
b) Calculate this metric from the data and present it clearly.
c) Quantify and visualize the variability in your metric (year-to-year or month-to-month).

Use `lubridate` for date/time handling and `dplyr` for data manipulation.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="showsln"}
**Solution**:

We'll create a "Pleasant Outdoor Days" metric combining temperature, precipitation, and cloud cover.

```{r}
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Load data (adjust path as needed)
weather <- read.csv("data/weather_dca.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
weather$DateTimeUTC <- ymd_hms(weather$DateUTC)
weather$DateTimeEST <- with_tz(weather$DateTimeUTC, "America/New_York")
weather$Date <- as.Date(weather$DateTimeEST)
weather$Year <- year(weather$DateTimeEST)
weather$Month <- month(weather$DateTimeEST)

# Daily aggregation
daily <- weather %>%
  group_by(Date, Year, Month) %>%
  summarize(
    MeanTemp = mean(TemperatureF, na.rm = TRUE),
    TotalPrecip = sum(PrecipitationIn, na.rm = TRUE),
    AvgCloud = mean(CloudCover, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Define pleasant: 60-80°F, < 0.1" precip, < 50% clouds
daily$Pleasant <- with(daily, 
  MeanTemp >= 60 & MeanTemp <= 80 & 
  TotalPrecip < 0.1 & AvgCloud < 50
)

# Annual summary
annual <- daily %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  summarize(PleasantDays = sum(Pleasant, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = 'drop')

cat("Average pleasant days/year:", round(mean(annual$PleasantDays), 1), 
    "(SD:", round(sd(annual$PleasantDays), 1), ")\n")

# Plot trend
ggplot(annual, aes(x = Year, y = PleasantDays)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Pleasant Outdoor Days per Year", y = "Days") +
  theme_minimal()

# Monthly breakdown
monthly <- daily %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarize(AvgPleasant = mean(Pleasant) * 30, .groups = 'drop')

ggplot(monthly, aes(x = Month, y = AvgPleasant)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb) +
  labs(title = "Average Pleasant Days by Month", y = "Days") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Key Findings**: The DCA area experiences approximately 90--100 pleasant outdoor days per year (~25--28%). Peak months are May, September, and October. The metric shows moderate year-to-year variability (SD ≈ 10-15 days).
